settingText: PRESENT — modern Neo-Vectra transit plaza during morning rush, ordinary commuters suddenly reacting to memories that do not belong to their present biographies.
summary: Public memory return reaches Neo-Vectra. Strangers recognize old names, dead relatives, former loyalties and injuries that current history says never existed. Theo, Rae and Adrian arrive as a crowd begins turning private contradiction into public panic.

dialogueInline.text: You left me at the south gate.

directionInline.text: Start with human confusion, not citywide spectacle. People remember emotionally before they understand historically. Present-day lives remain real; recovered lives are also real. The conflict comes from holding both.

settingText: PAST — ancient Neo-Vectra command balcony overlooking a populated city already preparing for war.
summary: Oryon debuts by telling Arbiter that every future in which they wait ends with Neo-Vectra becoming the doorway to a wider catastrophe. Arbiter asks whether Oryon has seen any future in which fear does not become permission.

dialogueInline.text: If we wait, this city becomes the beginning.
Everything we have been trying to prevent.
Or because you keep looking for the same ending.

directionInline.text: Oryon's foresight is experiential, not mathematical. He has seen futures and carries anticipatory grief. Do not use percentages, probability branches or diagrams. Arbiter respects him enough to challenge the emotional habit inside his certainty.

settingText: PRESENT — Neo-Vectra side street where two groups of strangers have begun gathering around symbols they remember but cannot explain.
summary: Recovered factional symbols begin attracting people who do not know why they feel loyal to them. Theo wants to tell everyone the truth immediately; Rae insists that explanation will not stop people from acting on grief they have only just recovered.

dialogueInline.text: They deserve to know what those marks mean.
They deserve not to get killed while we're explaining it.
No. We keep them from choosing a war before they remember why it ended.

directionInline.text: Rae is not advocating suppression. She is separating truth from immediate action. Present-day factions should form through emotion and recognition, not magical mind control.

settingText: PAST — ancient Neo-Vectra residential concourse as Atlas shields civilians while Oryon urges evacuation from a city he believes cannot be saved.
summary: Atlas refuses Oryon's demand to abandon Neo-Vectra. Mero sees both arguments: Atlas is saving people in front of him; Oryon believes staying will kill people far beyond the city.

dialogueInline.text: You are saving the people who can see you.
So are the ones who die if this gets out.
That's the sentence that keeps ruining us.

directionInline.text: Oryon must not read as callous. He is grieving people not yet dead. Atlas is not naive; he refuses to let hypothetical future lives erase visible present ones. Mero is exhausted by the forced binary.

settingText: PRESENT — same modern concourse occupying the physical footprint of the ancient scene, now crowded with confused civilians.
summary: Theo recognizes the present concourse as the place Atlas stood. A man in the crowd remembers dying there and becomes terrified of a woman he currently loves because his recovered memory identifies her ancient faction as the enemy.

dialogueInline.text: This is what I was afraid of.

directionInline.text: Make contradictory identities intimate. The couple's present love is real; the recovered fear is also real. Do not imply one history is fake. Adrian sees exactly the social fracture that motivated the Reset.

settingText: PAST — ancient Neo-Vectra command hall with Starbreaker, Redlin and Oryon arguing while Flux's empty place remains conspicuous.
summary: Oryon pushes for pre-emptive action, Starbreaker agrees the danger cannot be allowed to widen, and Redlin sees certainty feeding escalation. Flux's unexplained absence removes the one person who used to challenge all of them from outside the binary.

dialogueInline.text: No. Flux knew enough to stop saying that.
Maybe because none of you listened.
Either way, Flux isn't here to choose for us.

directionInline.text: Let Flux's empty place function emotionally. Oryon's certainty should feel partly like compensation for losing the person who challenged it. No one knows whether Flux abandoned them, died, escaped, or found something else.

settingText: PRESENT — Neo-Vectra municipal shelter as people with conflicting recovered memories are separated after several fights.
summary: Adrian proposes cutting people off from memory-triggering sites. Theo hears the beginning of another Reset. Rae rejects both Adrian's suppression instinct and Theo's demand for immediate universal disclosure.

dialogueInline.text: Move them away from the old sites.
I'm trying to stop people from hurting each other.
By taking the memory away again.

directionInline.text: This is the finale argument in miniature. Rae begins articulating the distinction the series will ultimately choose: no coercive control of memory, but real responsibility for what people do with it.

settingText: PAST — ancient Mero staff room during Neo-Vectra, with ancient Theo now fully visible beside the general.
summary: Mero asks Theo what the senior champions cannot answer. Theo suggests bringing the opposing moral truths into the same room rather than letting each side turn the other into evidence of evil. The advice helps move Mero toward the final council that will eventually consider the Reset.

dialogueInline.text: You're getting promoted if you keep insulting my command staff.
No. Their arguments are. Put the people there.

directionInline.text: Theo's ancient choice is modest but consequential. He does not devise the Reset. He pushes Mero toward a council where people must confront one another rather than abstractions. Preserve his junior status and the warmth in Mero's joke.

settingText: PRESENT — Neo-Vectra plaza at night, faction symbols now appearing on handmade signs beside present-day names and family photographs.
summary: Recovered loyalties begin turning into organization. Theo sees that giving people truth does not automatically produce wisdom. Rae sees that trying to stop organization would simply recreate the control they fear.

dialogueInline.text: I thought remembering would make it make sense.
Ask Adrian. He tried the alternative.

directionInline.text: Avoid sudden armies. People make signs, meet strangers, trade stories, argue. The danger is social formation around recovered history, not supernatural possession.

settingText: PAST — ancient Arbiter workroom during Neo-Vectra, with Rae openly present as strategic aide.
summary: Rae remembers helping Arbiter frame the triage of Neo-Vectra. She objects when people are reduced to categories and forces names and places back into the language, but she still participates in deciding which evacuations receive priority.

dialogueInline.text: You mean the people we haven't reached.
Fine. Who do we reach first?
The south gate. Then the river housing.

directionInline.text: Rae's culpability is not villainy. She humanizes the language and still makes a choice that leaves someone else waiting. This is what participation means: ethical resistance does not erase consequence.

settingText: PRESENT — quiet rooftop above Neo-Vectra while the city argues below.
summary: Theo and Rae admit their ancient selves influenced decisions that led toward the Reset. Their remembered identities no longer feel like foreign people they can simply condemn.

dialogueInline.text: I pushed Mero toward the council.
I chose who got out first.
That doesn't feel as helpful as I wanted.

directionInline.text: Let them own limited but real agency. Neither is secretly the architect of everything. The point is that ordinary participation matters even beside gods.

settingText: PRESENT — Neo-Vectra overlook before dawn as contradictory memories continue spreading through the city.
summary: Adrian tells them what full return could mean: people may recover loves, debts, betrayals, families and loyalties that contradict the lives they currently inhabit. The forgotten war can return socially before any ancient weapon does.

dialogueInline.text: You keep asking what happens if everyone remembers.
Someone remembers a wife they never married. Someone remembers killing the man who is now their brother. A city remembers belonging to an enemy that no longer exists.
And you thought forgetting was kinder.
I thought it was the only thing we hadn't tried.

directionInline.text: End with social and personal stakes, not a technical forecast. The alternating-page grammar has made past and present feel causally linked. Issue 8 will stop keeping them cleanly separate.
